The vast amount of structured data available on Wikipedia provides a rich source for entity recommendations. However, Wikipedia's inherent structure, comprising interconnected categories and entities, poses a challenge for traditional recommendation methods. To address this, we propose a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that leverages a layered graph embedding approach. This method utilizes Wikipedia's category and entity relationships to generate a two-level embedding, where category embeddings are used to derive entity embeddings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by integrating it into the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph and evaluating its performance on entity recommendations. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, including graph-based and knowledge graph embedding methods, in terms of recommendation accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of Wikipedia categories on entity recommendations and provide insights into the characteristics of Wikipedia entities and categories. Our findings indicate that Wikipedia categories play a crucial role in entity recommendations, and our proposed method can effectively capture this relationship. We also observe that Wikipedia entities and categories exhibit distinct characteristics, with entities being more densely connected within categories than categories being connected among themselves. When fine-tuning NLP models, the choice of hyperparameters significantly affects their performance. However, the process of selecting optimal hyperparameters is complicated by the inherent randomness of models, which leads to inconsistent results across different validation sets. This issue is particularly pronounced in NLP, where the scarcity of labeled data and the complexity of language models exacerbate the problem. As a result, the optimal hyperparameters often yield subpar performance on unseen data. To mitigate this, we propose a novel approach that incorporates a variant of k-fold cross-validation, which we call j-k fold CV. This method involves dividing the validation set into multiple subsets and training the model on each subset, thereby reducing the variance of hyperparameter selection. We demonstrate the efficacy of j-k fold CV through experiments on multiple NLP tasks, including text classification and named entity recognition. The results show that our approach yields more stable and accurate models, outperforming traditional k-fold CV and grid search methods. Furthermore, we found that j-k fold CV is particularly effective when the model's performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameters. We also provide a Python implementation of j-k fold CV as part of the Hyperopt library. Our findings suggest that j-k fold CV is a valuable tool for NLP practitioners seeking to optimize hyperparameters, especially when working with complex models and limited data. We believe that our approach can be adapted to other machine learning tasks and look forward to exploring its potential in future research. The concept of knowledge learning has gained significant attention in recent years, driven by the rapid growth of data and the increasing complexity of deep neural networks. The primary goal of knowledge learning is to enable a student model to acquire knowledge from a teacher model, thereby enhancing the student's performance and efficiency. This survey provides an in-depth examination of the teacher-student architecture, exploring its various components, including the teacher model, student model, knowledge distillation, and knowledge aggregation. We delve into the design principles and optimization techniques employed in these components, as well as the applications of teacher-student architectures in computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential solutions in knowledge learning, including the development of more sophisticated teacher models, the optimization of knowledge aggregation, and the exploration of new knowledge distillation methods. This survey aims to facilitate further research in knowledge learning by offering a comprehensive overview of the field and highlighting promising directions for future investigation. We also provide a publicly accessible repository of code and pre-trained models to support the reproducibility of our findings. This survey is an extension of our earlier work, featuring an expanded discussion of knowledge learning and the teacher-student architecture, as well as the inclusion of new research and methodologies. This updated survey is intended to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of knowledge learning. utilizing a hydrodynamic approach that incorporates a dissipation mechanism. 
Our analysis reveals that the Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the viscosity 
and inversely proportional to the entropy carried by quasiparticles, 
with a proportionality constant determined by quasiparticle mobility. 
This relationship is applicable to both normal and superconducting states. 
In the vortex liquid regime, the quasiparticle mobility is significantly reduced, 
resulting in a substantial increase in the Nernst coefficient. 
This enhancement is attributed to the increased entropy carried by quasiparticles, 
which is a direct consequence of quasiparticle mobility being reduced. 
This finding is supported by numerical simulations of the vortex liquid state. 
Our results demonstrate that the Nernst coefficient can be used as a sensitive probe 
of quasiparticle mobility and entropy in vortex liquids.

Modern cloud applications are comprised of multiple interconnected microservices, 
which are typically deployed within isolated containers. To ensure the security of 
these applications, system call policies must be implemented at the container level. 
However, manually configuring these policies for each container is a time-consuming 
and labor-intensive process. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach 
called Timeloops, which utilizes machine learning to automate the process of creating 
system call policies for containerized microservices. By analyzing system call 
patterns, Timeloops creates a temporal graph representation of each service's system 
call behavior, which is then used to train a graph-based classifier. This classifier 
is capable of accurately identifying malicious system calls and predicting the 
temporal patterns of system call sequences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of 
Timeloops through a comprehensive evaluation of real-world containerized applications, 
which shows that our approach outperforms existing methods by a significant margin.

performance of Timeloops and explore the potential of our approach to be applied to

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on multiple datasets, including the widely used MiniImageNet and tiered-ImageNet benchmarks, as well as a new dataset featuring a diverse set of tasks. Our results show that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing unsupervised generalization techniques, including those that employ additional supervision. Notably, our method's performance is particularly impressive when the number of available training samples is limited. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of our method's components and explore its potential applications in real-world scenarios. Reward function learning is a crucial step in reinforcement learning, enabling the efficient exploration of complex environments. However, designing an effective reward function requires significant human expertise and time. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Visually Assisted Cluster Ranking (VACR), which leverages human feedback to rapidly learn a reward function. VACR utilizes a compact, high-level representation of the environment's state space, dividing it into clusters that are easily understandable to humans. By ranking these clusters based on their desirability, humans provide a concise and interpretable form of feedback. We demonstrate VACR's efficacy in learning reward functions for complex tasks, including robotic grasping and navigation, with human feedback that is 10-20 times more concise than traditional methods. Our results show that VACR achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly less human time and effort. By streamlining the reward learning process, VACR has the potential to accelerate the development of more efficient reinforcement learning algorithms. the maximum expected loss across all possible data distributions, subject to certain
constraints. However, solving this problem is computationally infeasible due to the
need to optimize over an infinite number of possible distributions. To address this

variant of the distributionally robust federated learning algorithm DSGD. DR-DSGD

phase. During the local optimization phase, each node optimizes its local model using
a distributionally robust objective function, which is a convex relaxation of the

update step, where each node updates its model based on the gradient of the local
model. We prove that DR-DSGD converges at a rate of O(1/T) under certain conditions,

dataset and a real-world dataset. The results show that DR-DSGD outperforms the

We investigate wave propagation in finite, non-reciprocal PT-symmetric photonic lattices, focusing on the interplay between symmetry and periodic structure. Contrary to expectations, we find that PT symmetry does not guarantee unidirectional light flow, and instead, we observe bidirectional transparency in these systems. This phenomenon is further enhanced by the presence of a PT-symmetric defect, which enables the creation of a coherent perfect absorber or lasing device. Notably, the PT-symmetric defect's performance is unaffected by the system's size, and we demonstrate this robustness through numerical simulations. Additionally, we explore the impact of symmetry breaking on these systems, revealing that it can lead to the emergence of a unidirectional light flow regime. This research provides valuable insights into the complex behavior of PT-symmetric photonic lattices and highlights the potential of these systems for the development of novel optical devices. Furthermore, our findings have implications for the study of PT-symmetric systems, underscoring the importance of considering the interplay between symmetry and boundary conditions. The Minimum Uncovered Union (MUC) measure has been successfully applied to evaluate feature importance in decision trees. This study extends the MUC measure to assess feature importance in Random Forest ensembles by aggregating individual MUC scores. We also investigate the robustness of the MUC measure to adversarial attacks on Random Forest models, demonstrating that the MUC scores of critical features remain relatively stable even when the model is compromised. This finding suggests that the MUC measure can be a reliable indicator of feature importance in Random Forest models, including those that have been compromised by adversarial attacks. This research also provides a Python implementation of the MUC measure for Random Forest models. Furthermore, we propose a new method for identifying the most critical features in a dataset, which we call the MUC-driven Feature Importance Measurement and Adversarial Analysis (MFI3A) method. This method involves generating a set of adversarially trained models, computing the MUC scores for each feature, and then ranking the features based on their average MUC scores. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the MFI3A method on several datasets, including a real-world dataset related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The results show that the MFI3A method can identify the most critical features in a dataset, even when the model has been compromised by adversarial attacks. This research provides a new approach for evaluating feature importance in Random Forest models, which can be applied to a wide range of applications, including data preprocessing, feature selection, and model interpretability. The increasing complexity of modern knowledge representation systems necessitates the incorporation of domain-specific knowledge from unstructured text sources. This paper introduces a novel approach to ontology enrichment, leveraging a deep learning model to extract relevant information from unstructured texts. By integrating the model with an existing ontology, we demonstrate its effectiveness in refining the ontology by adding new concepts, relationships, and attributes. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms traditional methods, achieving a 25% improvement in precision and a 30% increase in recall. Furthermore, we present a case study on enriching the SUMO ontology using Wikipedia articles, resulting in the addition of 1,500 new concepts, 2,500 new relationships, and 1,000 new attributes. This research contributes to the advancement of knowledge representation systems and the development of more sophisticated AI applications. The proposed approach is made available as an open-source framework, enabling the extension of existing ontologies with domain-specific knowledge from unstructured text sources. Deep learning models, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks. However, their widespread adoption in safety-critical applications is hindered by the lack of a comprehensive safety framework. This study focuses on developing a safety framework for CNNs, specifically addressing hardware faults that can compromise their reliability. We introduce a novel approach called Activation Range Supervision (ARS), which ensures the output of a CNN remains within a predetermined range despite hardware faults. ARS is a lightweight, low-overhead method that can be applied to existing CNNs without requiring significant modifications. We demonstrate the efficacy of ARS through experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, showcasing its ability to prevent erroneous outputs caused by hardware faults. Furthermore, we present a safety case for ARS, which includes a hazard analysis, risk assessment, and mitigation strategy. This safety case provides a foundation for the development of a comprehensive safety framework for CNNs. We also discuss the limitations of our approach and potential avenues for future research. This work is a step towards creating a safety framework for CNNs, which is essential for their adoption in safety-critical applications. To enhance the efficiency of cross-lingual learning, we propose a novel method to create a shared semantic space across multiple languages. This approach leverages a clustering-based word embedding technique to ensure that words with similar meanings are grouped together, and then utilizes a consistent clustering framework to align clusters across languages. By minimizing the differences in cluster structures, our method effectively bridges the gap between languages and enables the creation of a shared semantic space. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in cross-lingual learning tasks, including bilingual dictionary induction and text classification. Notably, our method excels in low-resource language settings, showcasing its potential to facilitate cross-lingual learning. Dialogue state tracking is a crucial component of dialogue management, yet it's hindered by the presence of noisy labels. This issue is particularly pronounced in datasets with high label noise rates, which can lead to subpar performance and unreliable evaluation metrics. To address this challenge, we introduce the ASSIST framework, which leverages a robust evaluation metric to identify noisy labels and a noise-aware loss function to optimize model performance. By incorporating a noise-robust training objective, ASSIST enables the model to learn from noisy labels while resisting overfitting. Experimental results on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of ASSIST, achieving a 4.3% improvement in F1 score compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of label noise on dialogue state tracking and propose a novel evaluation metric, the robust F1 score, to assess model performance in the presence of noisy labels. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/THU-ICST/ASSIST.

The detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and VIRGO collaboration has opened a new avenue for astronomy, enabling the study of cosmic phenomena through wave patterns. However, the analysis of these signals is hindered by the vast amount of data generated by the detectors, necessitating the development of sophisticated algorithms to identify and classify gravitational wave events. In this study, we employ deep learning techniques to enhance the performance of existing algorithms, specifically the PyANITA software, which is used to detect and classify neutron star-black hole merger signals. Our results demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses the capabilities of PyANITA, achieving a 25% increase in detection accuracy and a 50% reduction in false positives. Furthermore, our model exhibits a 10% improvement in classification accuracy for binary black hole mergers, a 20% improvement for neutron star-black hole mergers, and a 30% improvement for neutron star-neutron star mergers. Our research contributes to the advancement of PyANITA and other similar algorithms, paving the way for the development of more sophisticated and efficient methods for gravitational wave detection and analysis. Our findings also underscore the potential of deep learning to tackle complex problems in astrophysics and cosmology. Through extensive experiments on the COCO dataset, we demonstrate that FourierMask outperforms state-of-the-art instance segmentation methods, including those utilizing explicit networks. To address this issue, we introduce SPACE-2, a novel tree-structured semi-supervised contrastive pre-training framework that leverages unlabeled data to enhance the robustness of pre-trained models. In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents are trained to excel in multiple tasks simultaneously, leveraging shared knowledge to enhance performance. However, when the tasks are highly dissimilar, the agent's ability to learn from one task is hindered by its learning from another, a phenomenon known as catastrophic interference. To address this challenge, we propose a novel model-based multi-task reinforcement learning framework that utilizes modular networks to prevent catastrophic interference. By incorporating a separate model for each task, our framework enables the agent to learn from each task independently, thereby reducing interference and facilitating the sharing of knowledge across tasks. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on complex, high-dimensional tasks, including a challenging robotic grasping scenario, and show that our framework outperforms existing methods in terms of both efficiency and performance. Notably, our approach achieves a 25% improvement in grasping success rates compared to the next best method, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the benefits of our modular network design. Our code is available at https://github.com/eth-srl/mbmtl. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark for evaluating multi-task reinforcement learning methods, which can be found at https://github.com/eth-srl/mbmtl-benchmark. Our work offers a novel perspective on the role of model-based methods in multi-task reinforcement learning and highlights the potential of modular networks to mitigate catastrophic interference. We believe that our framework and benchmark will serve as valuable resources for the broader reinforcement learning community. Speech synthesis has seen significant advancements with neural network-based approaches, particularly those rooted in sequence-to-sequence architectures. However, these models often struggle with raw waveform generation due to the high sampling rates and the need for precise timing control. To address this challenge, we introduce the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, a novel autoregressive raw waveform generative model that leverages a pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural network to capture the inherent periodicity of speech. By incorporating a pitch-dependent dilated convolution layer, our model effectively reduces the number of parameters required, enabling efficient training and generation of high-quality speech waveforms. Experimental results demonstrate that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet outperforms existing methods in terms of waveform generation, with a notable improvement in the mean opinion score (MOS) of 0.16 compared to the baseline WaveNet. Furthermore, our model achieves comparable text-to-speech synthesis performance to sequence-to-sequence models, as evidenced by the MOS scores of 4.44 and 4.35, respectively.
